title: Hardcoded Credentials / Secrets
description: Embedding credentials, API keys, or secrets directly in source code exposes them to anyone with access to the repository, build artifacts, logs, or error messages.
rule: Secrets must never appear as literals in source code or version-controlled configuration files.

source.name: OWASP Top 10:2025 — A07
source.title: A07:2025 – Authentication Failures

evidence: OWASP A07:2025 (Authentication Failures) identifies 'uses default, weak, or well-known passwords' and 'stores passwords in plain text or with weak encryption' as primary failure patterns. Hardcoded credentials are a direct instance of this failure mode.
remediation: Load secrets from environment variables (os.environ), a secrets manager (AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault, Azure Key Vault, GCP Secret Manager), or an encrypted .env file not committed to version control. Rotate any exposed credentials immediately.
verification: Run a secrets-scanner (e.g., truffleHog, detect-secrets, git-secrets) against the repository including git history. Verify no plaintext secrets appear in CI logs or Docker image layers.
license_note: OWASP content is licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0

title: SQL Injection
description: SQL injection occurs when untrusted user input is incorporated into a database query without proper sanitization, allowing attackers to manipulate the query logic.
rule: Never construct SQL queries by concatenating or formatting user-controlled strings. Always use parameterized queries or prepared statements.

source.name: OWASP Cheat Sheet Series — SQL Injection Prevention
source.title: SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet

evidence: The OWASP SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet states: 'The use of prepared statements with variable binding (aka parameterized queries) is how all developers should first be taught how to write database queries.' It lists string concatenation as a primary attack vector that prepared statements eliminate.
example: query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name='" + username + "'"
remediation: Use parameterized queries: cursor.execute('SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = %s', (username,)). For ORMs, use the framework's built-in query builder rather than raw string interpolation.
verification: Test the endpoint with the payload: ' OR '1'='1. If the query returns unexpected results, the fix is incomplete. Use a DAST tool (e.g., OWASP ZAP) to confirm parameterized queries are enforced.
license_note: OWASP content is licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0

title: OS Command Injection
description: OS command injection occurs when user-controlled data is passed to a shell command, allowing an attacker to execute arbitrary system commands.
rule: Never pass user-controlled input directly to OS commands. Avoid shell=True. Use subprocess with argument lists and strict input validation.

source.name: OWASP Cheat Sheet Series — OS Command Injection Defense
source.title: OS Command Injection Defense Cheat Sheet

evidence: The OWASP OS Command Injection Defense Cheat Sheet states its primary defense as: 'Defense Option 1: Avoid calling OS commands directly.' When OS commands are unavoidable, it mandates parameterization and strict allow-list input validation, and explicitly warns that shell=True / string interpolation creates injection vectors.
remediation: Replace with subprocess.run(['ping', user_input], shell=False). Validate user_input against an explicit allow-list before use. Prefer library functions over shell commands where possible.
verification: Test with payloads such as: ; cat /etc/passwd or && whoami. If the command executes the payload, the vulnerability is unmitigated. Run static analysis (Bandit for Python) to detect shell=True usage.
license_note: OWASP content is licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0

title: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
description: XSS occurs when untrusted data is included in a web page without proper encoding, allowing attackers to inject malicious scripts that execute in victims' browsers.
rule: All user-controlled data rendered in HTML responses must be output-encoded for the correct context (HTML, JavaScript, CSS, URL). Never trust raw user input in rendering pipelines.

source.name: OWASP Cheat Sheet Series — Cross Site Scripting Prevention
source.title: Cross Site Scripting Prevention Cheat Sheet

evidence: The OWASP XSS Prevention Cheat Sheet states: 'Never Insert Untrusted Data Except in Allowed Locations' and defines context-specific output encoding rules (HTML entity encoding, JavaScript encoding, CSS encoding, URL encoding) as the primary defense. It explicitly classifies innerHTML and document.write as dangerous sinks.
remediation: Use textContent instead of innerHTML for plain text. Apply context-appropriate escaping libraries (e.g., Jinja2 auto-escaping, OWASP Java Encoder). Set Content-Security-Policy headers as a defense-in-depth measure.
verification: Test with the payload: <script>alert(1)</script>. If the script executes, output encoding is missing. Use an automated scanner (OWASP ZAP) to test for reflected and stored XSS.
license_note: OWASP content is licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0

title: Path Traversal
owasp_ref: OWASP Top 10:2025 A01 – Broken Access Control
description: Path traversal allows an attacker to construct file paths (e.g., using ../../) that escape the intended directory, accessing or overwriting arbitrary files on the server.
rule: Validate and canonicalize all file paths constructed from user input. Confirm the resolved path lies within the intended base directory before accessing the file.

source.name: OWASP Cheat Sheet Series — Path Traversal
source.title: Path Traversal Cheat Sheet

evidence: The OWASP Path Traversal Cheat Sheet states that path traversal (or directory traversal) vulnerabilities allow an attacker to read arbitrary files on the server running an application. Per MITRE CWE-22 (maintained by MITRE, not OWASP): 'The product uses external input to construct a pathname intended to identify a file or directory… but the product does not properly neutralize special elements within the pathname.'
remediation: Use os.path.realpath() to resolve the canonical path, then assert it starts with the expected base directory prefix. Reject requests where the resolved path escapes the base. Use allow-lists for file extensions.
verification: Test with the filename: ../../etc/passwd. If the server returns the file contents, path traversal is present. Use OWASP ZAP or Burp Suite path traversal scanner.
license_note: OWASP content is licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0; CWE is maintained by MITRE

title: Missing Authentication
description: Critical functionality is accessible without any authentication check, allowing any unauthenticated user or attacker to invoke privileged operations.
rule: Every endpoint that accesses sensitive data or performs privileged operations must require valid authentication before proceeding.

source.name: OWASP Cheat Sheet Series — Authentication
source.title: Authentication Cheat Sheet

evidence: The OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet states: 'All pages and resources should be protected, except those specifically intended to be public.' It further requires authentication checks to be performed server-side for every request to a protected resource.
remediation: Apply an authentication decorator, middleware, or guard to every protected endpoint. Validate the session token or JWT server-side. In frameworks like FastAPI, use Depends() with a security scheme.
verification: Make an unauthenticated request (no Authorization header / no session cookie) to the endpoint. If it returns 200 OK with data, authentication is missing. Automate with OWASP ZAP authentication scan.
license_note: OWASP content is licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0

title: Broken Authorization / Access Control
owasp_ref: OWASP Top 10:2025 A01 – Broken Access Control
description: Access control failures occur when authenticated users can access resources or perform actions beyond their intended permissions, commonly via Insecure Direct Object References (IDOR) or missing role checks.
rule: Enforce authorization checks on every resource access. Verify that the authenticated user has explicit permission to access or modify the requested resource — do not rely solely on obscurity.

source.name: OWASP Cheat Sheet Series — Authorization
source.title: Authorization Cheat Sheet

evidence: The OWASP Authorization Cheat Sheet states: 'Enforce authorization on every request' and 'Verify that the user is authorized to access the specific resource, not just the resource type.' OWASP A01:2025 lists IDOR and missing function-level access control as the top-ranked application security risk.
remediation: After authentication, check that the authenticated user owns or has explicit permission to access the requested object: assert invoice.owner_id == current_user.id. Use a centralized authorization library or middleware.
verification: Log in as User A, obtain a resource ID (e.g., invoice_id=42), then log in as User B and directly request /api/invoice/42. If User B can access User A's resource, IDOR is confirmed.
license_note: OWASP content is licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0

title: Insecure Password Storage
description: Passwords stored using weak, reversible, or unsalted cryptographic hashing algorithms (e.g., MD5, SHA-1, unsalted SHA-256) can be cracked rapidly using rainbow tables or brute-force attacks.
rule: Passwords must be stored using a dedicated, slow, salted password-hashing algorithm: bcrypt, Argon2id, or PBKDF2 with a sufficient iteration count.

source.name: OWASP Cheat Sheet Series — Password Storage
source.title: Password Storage Cheat Sheet

evidence: The OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet states: 'Use Argon2id... bcrypt... or PBKDF2' and explicitly classifies MD5, SHA-1, and SHA-256 as 'NOT suitable for password storage' because they are designed for speed rather than resistance to brute-force attacks.
remediation: Use bcrypt (passlib.hash.bcrypt) or Argon2id (argon2-cffi). Example: from argon2 import PasswordHasher; ph = PasswordHasher(); hash = ph.hash(password). Migrate existing MD5/SHA-1 hashes on next user login.
verification: Retrieve a stored password hash and identify the algorithm prefix ($2b$ = bcrypt, $argon2id$ = Argon2). If no prefix or a raw hex digest is present, the algorithm is insecure.
license_note: OWASP content is licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0

title: Sensitive Information Exposure
owasp_ref: OWASP Cheat Sheet Series (Sensitive Information Exposure is not a standalone category in OWASP Top 10:2025)
description: Sensitive data (credentials, PII, financial data, session tokens) is logged, returned in API responses, or exposed in error messages, making it accessible to attackers.
rule: Never log or expose sensitive fields in responses, logs, or error messages. Scrub sensitive data before logging. Return minimal error information to clients.

source.name: OWASP Cheat Sheet Series — Logging
source.title: Logging Cheat Sheet

evidence: The OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet explicitly warns against logging sensitive data such as credentials, session tokens, personal data (PII), and financial information. CWE-200 (Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor, maintained by MITRE) defines the risk of leaking sensitive technical or personal details in application outputs, logs, or error messages.
remediation: Remove sensitive fields from log statements. Use structured logging with field-level redaction. Return generic error messages to clients; log detailed errors server-side only. Use HTTPS for all data in transit.
verification: Review log output after a login or payment operation. Search for patterns matching passwords, tokens, card numbers, SSNs. Confirm API error responses do not include stack traces or internal field names.
license_note: OWASP content is licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0

title: Security Misconfiguration
description: Security misconfiguration results from insecure default settings, incomplete configuration, open cloud storage, verbose error messages, or unnecessary features being left enabled in production.
rule: Harden all configurations for production. Disable debug mode, set strong secret keys, restrict CORS, and remove or disable unnecessary features, endpoints, and default credentials.

source.name: OWASP Top 10:2025 — A02
source.title: A02:2025 – Security Misconfiguration

evidence: OWASP A02:2025 (Security Misconfiguration) identifies 'unnecessary features are enabled or installed (e.g. unnecessary ports, services, pages, accounts, or privileges)' and 'error handling reveals stack traces or other overly informative error messages to users' as primary indicators of security misconfiguration.
remediation: Set DEBUG=False in production. Use environment-specific configuration files. Set a cryptographically random SECRET_KEY. Restrict CORS to known origins. Remove default accounts and sample applications.
verification: Deploy to a staging environment and verify: debug mode is off, error pages show generic messages, CORS headers are restricted, no default credentials exist, and unnecessary endpoints are disabled.
license_note: OWASP content is licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0

title: Insecure Cryptography
description: Use of deprecated or cryptographically weak algorithms (MD5, SHA-1, DES, RC4, ECB mode, 1024-bit RSA) makes encrypted data recoverable by an attacker with moderate resources.
rule: Use only currently recommended cryptographic algorithms and key sizes as specified in NIST guidelines. Avoid deprecated algorithms regardless of legacy compatibility arguments.

source.name: OWASP Cheat Sheet Series — Cryptographic Storage
source.title: Cryptographic Storage Cheat Sheet

evidence: The OWASP Cryptographic Storage Cheat Sheet explicitly lists MD5, SHA-1, DES, 3DES, and RC4 as algorithms that 'MUST NOT be used' for cryptographic operations. It recommends AES-256-GCM for symmetric encryption and SHA-256+ for hashing (non-password) use cases.
remediation: Use AES-256-GCM for symmetric encryption (from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.aead import AESGCM). For asymmetric encryption, use RSA-2048+ or ECC P-256+. For general hashing, use SHA-256 or SHA-3.
verification: Audit all cryptographic algorithm references in the codebase. Search for deprecated module imports (Crypto.Cipher.DES, hashlib.md5). Run a SAST tool (Bandit, Semgrep) with crypto-specific rules.
license_note: OWASP content is licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0

title: Weak Session Management
description: Weak session management — including predictable session IDs, missing cookie security flags, absent session expiry, or JWT algorithm confusion — allows session hijacking or token forgery.
rule: Session tokens must be unpredictable, transmitted only over HTTPS, expire after inactivity, and be invalidated on logout. JWTs must be signed with a strong algorithm (RS256 or HS256 with a strong secret).

source.name: OWASP Cheat Sheet Series — Session Management
source.title: Session Management Cheat Sheet

evidence: The OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet specifies: 'The session ID must be at least 128 bits long', 'cookies must use the Secure, HttpOnly, and SameSite attributes', and 'session expiration must be enforced both on the server side and via cookie Max-Age'. It also requires session ID regeneration after privilege changes.
remediation: Use a proven session library. Set HttpOnly=True, Secure=True, SameSite=Lax on all session cookies. Generate session IDs using os.urandom(32). Implement server-side session expiry. For JWTs, reject the 'none' algorithm.
verification: Inspect the session cookie: verify HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite flags are set. Verify token entropy (should not be sequential or predictable). For JWTs, verify the alg header is not 'none' and the signature is validated.
license_note: OWASP content is licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0

title: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF)
owasp_ref: OWASP Cheat Sheet Series (SSRF is not a standalone category in OWASP Top 10:2025)
description: SSRF occurs when a server makes HTTP requests to user-controlled URLs, allowing attackers to probe internal services, cloud metadata endpoints, or other backend infrastructure.
rule: Never make server-side HTTP requests to user-supplied URLs without strict validation. Use an allow-list of permitted schemes and hostnames. Block access to internal IP ranges.

source.name: OWASP Cheat Sheet Series — SSRF Prevention
source.title: Server Side Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet

evidence: The OWASP SSRF Prevention Cheat Sheet specifies that 'an allow-list approach must be used to validate the destination URL' and that developers must 'block requests to private IP addresses (RFC 1918), loopback addresses, and cloud metadata endpoints (e.g. 169.254.169.254).'
remediation: Validate the user-supplied URL against an explicit allow-list of permitted domains and schemes. Resolve the hostname and check it against a deny-list of private/loopback ranges before making the request. Use a dedicated HTTP client with disable_redirects=True.
verification: Test by submitting http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ as the URL. If the server returns cloud metadata, SSRF is confirmed. Also test with http://localhost/ and http://192.168.1.1/.
license_note: OWASP content is licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0

title: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)
owasp_ref: OWASP Top 10:2025 A01 – Broken Access Control
description: CSRF tricks authenticated users into submitting forged requests from attacker-controlled pages, causing the server to execute unintended state-changing operations using the victim's credentials.
rule: Protect all state-changing requests with CSRF tokens or enforce SameSite cookie attributes. Verify the Origin/Referer header as a defence-in-depth measure.

source.name: OWASP Cheat Sheet Series — Cross-Site Request Forgery Prevention
source.title: Cross-Site Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet

evidence: The OWASP CSRF Prevention Cheat Sheet defines the primary defence as synchronizer token pattern: 'The CSRF token must be unique per user session, large enough to be unpredictable, and validated server-side on every state-changing request.' It also mandates SameSite=Lax or Strict on session cookies.
remediation: Use your framework's built-in CSRF protection (e.g., Flask-WTF, Django's {% csrf_token %}). Set SameSite=Lax on session cookies. Validate the Origin or Referer header for API endpoints.
verification: Create an HTML page on a different origin containing a form that POSTs to the protected endpoint. Submit the form as an authenticated user. If the action succeeds without a valid CSRF token, the protection is missing.
license_note: OWASP content is licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0

title: Insecure Deserialization
owasp_ref: OWASP Top 10:2025 A08 – Software or Data Integrity Failures
description: Deserializing data from untrusted sources using unsafe libraries (e.g., Python pickle, Java ObjectInputStream, unsafe YAML.load) can allow attackers to execute arbitrary code.
rule: Never deserialize data from untrusted sources using formats that support arbitrary object instantiation (pickle, marshal, Java native serialization). Use safe formats (JSON, MessagePack) with schema validation.

source.name: OWASP Cheat Sheet Series — Deserialization
source.title: Deserialization Cheat Sheet

evidence: The OWASP Deserialization Cheat Sheet states: 'Avoid native deserialization formats... Pickle is inherently insecure and should not be used to deserialize data from untrusted sources.' It classifies Python pickle, PHP unserialize, and Java ObjectInputStream as high-risk when accepting external data.
remediation: Replace pickle with json.loads() for data exchange. If a binary format is required, use MessagePack or Protocol Buffers with schema validation. If pickle is unavoidable, use cryptographic signing to ensure the data originated from a trusted source.
verification: Craft a pickle payload that executes os.system('id') and submit it to the endpoint. If the command executes, the vulnerability is confirmed. Review code for any pickle.loads() or yaml.load() call that accepts external data.
license_note: OWASP content is licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0

title: Dangerous File Upload
owasp_ref: OWASP Top 10:2025 A01 – Broken Access Control
description: Accepting file uploads without validating file type, content, and storage location allows attackers to upload malicious files (web shells, malware) that execute on the server.
rule: Validate uploaded files by magic number (not just extension or MIME type header). Store uploads outside the web root. Rename files to server-generated names. Restrict executable file types.

source.name: OWASP Cheat Sheet Series — File Upload
source.title: File Upload Cheat Sheet

evidence: The OWASP File Upload Cheat Sheet states: 'Ensure the file is not executable by the web server', 'validate using both extension and magic number checks', and 'store files outside of the webroot.' It classifies unrestricted file upload as enabling remote code execution.
remediation: Validate the file's magic bytes (use python-magic). Reject executable extensions (.php, .py, .sh, .js server-side). Rename files to a UUID. Store uploads in a directory outside the web root, served via a dedicated file-serving endpoint.
verification: Upload a file named shell.php containing <?php system($_GET['cmd']); ?>. If the server stores it and makes it accessible at a URL that executes PHP, the vulnerability is present.
license_note: OWASP content is licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0

title: Missing Rate Limiting
description: Without rate limiting on authentication and sensitive endpoints, attackers can perform brute-force or credential-stuffing attacks to compromise accounts.
rule: Apply rate limiting to all authentication endpoints, password reset flows, and sensitive API operations. Implement account lockout or CAPTCHA after repeated failures.

source.name: OWASP Cheat Sheet Series — Authentication
source.title: Authentication Cheat Sheet — Protect Against Automated Attacks

evidence: The OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet section 'Protect Against Automated Attacks' states: 'Implement Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA)... Use CAPTCHA... Implement a temporary account lockout policy' to defend against brute-force and credential-stuffing attacks. It recommends a maximum of 5 failed attempts before a lockout.
remediation: Apply rate limiting middleware (e.g., slowapi for FastAPI, Flask-Limiter). Implement exponential backoff and account lockout after 5–10 failed attempts. Add CAPTCHA for public-facing authentication.
verification: Send 100 sequential login requests with incorrect passwords. If all requests are processed without throttling or lockout, rate limiting is absent.
license_note: OWASP content is licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0

title: Debug / Verbose Error Exposure
description: Exposing detailed error messages, stack traces, or debug information to clients reveals internal implementation details, file paths, and library versions that assist attackers in reconnaissance.
rule: Production systems must never return stack traces or internal error details to clients. Log errors server-side and return generic error messages.

source.name: OWASP Top 10:2025 — A02
source.title: A02:2025 – Security Misconfiguration

evidence: OWASP A02:2025 (Security Misconfiguration) lists 'error handling reveals stack traces or other overly informative error messages to users' as a primary indicator of security misconfiguration. CWE-209 (Generation of Error Message Containing Sensitive Information) documents how stack traces expose file paths, library versions, and internal logic.
remediation: Catch all exceptions at the top level and return a generic '500 Internal Server Error' with a correlation ID. Log the full stack trace server-side keyed to the correlation ID. Disable DEBUG mode in production.
verification: Trigger an unhandled exception (e.g., by sending malformed input) and inspect the response body. If the response contains a Python traceback, file paths, or library names, the fix is needed.
license_note: OWASP content is licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0; CWE is maintained by MITRE

title: Software Supply-Chain / Dependency Risk
owasp_ref: OWASP Top 10:2025 A03 – Software Supply Chain Failures
description: Using outdated, vulnerable, or unverified third-party packages introduces known CVEs and supply-chain attack vectors directly into the application.
rule: Track all direct and transitive dependencies. Regularly audit for known CVEs. Pin dependency versions. Verify package integrity (checksums/signatures).

source.name: OWASP Top 10:2025 — A03
source.title: A03:2025 – Software Supply Chain Failures

evidence: OWASP A03:2025 (Software Supply Chain Failures) covers vulnerable and outdated third-party components as a primary attack vector. It identifies failure to scan for known CVEs, track transitive dependencies, and promptly fix or upgrade vulnerable components as the core risk patterns.
remediation: Run pip-audit or safety check against requirements.txt as part of CI. Use Dependabot or Renovate to automate dependency updates. Pin versions with hashes in requirements.txt. Remove unused dependencies.
verification: Run: pip-audit -r requirements.txt. All reported CVEs must be remediated or formally accepted. Confirm the CI pipeline fails on new critical CVEs.
license_note: OWASP content is licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0

title: Insecure Randomness
description: Using non-cryptographic random functions (Python's random module, Math.random() in JavaScript) for security-sensitive values (session IDs, CSRF tokens, password reset tokens) makes those values predictable and forgeable.
rule: Use a cryptographically secure random number generator (CSPRNG) for all security-sensitive values: secrets.token_hex(), os.urandom(), or the platform's CSPRNG equivalent.

source.name: OWASP Cheat Sheet Series — Cryptographic Storage
source.title: Cryptographic Storage Cheat Sheet

evidence: The OWASP Cryptographic Storage Cheat Sheet specifies: 'Use a cryptographically secure pseudo-random number generator (CSPRNG)... Do not use language-level functions like Math.random() or random.random() for security-sensitive operations, as they are not cryptographically secure.'
remediation: Replace with: import secrets; token = secrets.token_hex(32). This uses the OS CSPRNG (os.urandom under the hood). For UUIDs, use uuid.uuid4() which is cryptographically random.
verification: Identify all uses of the random module or Math.random() in security-sensitive paths (token generation, session IDs, nonces). Confirm each is replaced with secrets.token_hex() or os.urandom(). Run Bandit (B311 rule) to detect insecure random usage.
license_note: OWASP content is licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0
